<reason>Both sides argued the motion as written and clashed cleanly, but B built the more decidable case. B anticipated the "most new commitments" wording early [B1.7] and then, under pressure, converted that apparent escape hatch into a genuine constraint by relocating the bar from category to financing ("paid for," not "sounds productive") [B4.4–B4.6], which directly defused A's strongest structural attack that PRO was just exempting its favorites [A2.1]. B also answered A's pressure question with a concrete, falsifiable trigger (full employment → primary balance, already fired) that costs B something, while A, asked for any threshold, offered only a dynamic r-vs-g test whose practical answer is always "keep investing." A's defense of that refusal (Japan, false precision) is intellectually respectable but leaves B's memorable frame — "can either side's rule ever say no?" — largely intact. B's dismantling of the WWII analogy (primary surpluses, inverted demographics, financial repression) and of the Eurozone comparison (cutting into a depression without a currency, versus consolidating at full employment) were the sharpest single exchanges; A's reply that "the mechanism is unaffected" restated the denominator claim without engaging r>g. A's late move to reclassify unfunded tax-cut extensions and benefit expansions as "legacy law" narrowed the motion in a way B exposed as definitional ("an expiring provision is a choice"), and A, speaking last, never answered it. A's closing also overclaimed that PRO "never rebutted" the productive-versus-consumption distinction, which B had in fact engaged via the accumulated-flow and pay-for arguments. A retains a live point — that a rule indifferent to what money buys can worsen the ratio — which keeps this competitive rather than lopsided.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's second rebuttal recasting the "higher bar" as a financing test rather than a category preference [B4.4–B4.6], which neutralized A's escape-hatch charge while simultaneously converting A's refusal to name any threshold into "a claim that the bill never arrives" — reinforced in closing by exposing the "legacy law" carve-out as defining away the biggest fights in Congress.</best_rebuttal>
